source: CSR-2 — Appendix B scripts, published third edition (PRE-EXISTING — published book content)

records.what_to_say: "You're not stupid — you're stuck. Those are very different things. Stuck is temporary, and we can get unstuck together. What's the part that feels hardest?"
records.what_not_to_say: "Don't say that about yourself!" (Dismissing the feeling teaches them to hide it.)
records.one_action: Separate identity from the moment — "You're a kid having a hard time with this problem. Let's look at just the next step."
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — "I'm stupid."

records.what_to_say: "That sounds really lonely. I'm sorry today felt like that. Tell me what happened — and remember, feeling left out sometimes doesn't mean nobody likes you. Who's someone who's usually kind to you?"
records.what_not_to_say: "That's not true, you have lots of friends!" (Arguing with their feelings shuts down the conversation.)
records.one_action: Plan one small social step — invite one kid for one low-pressure activity this week.
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — "Nobody likes me."

records.situation: "I don't want to try. I'll be bad at it."
records.what_to_say: "You might be bad at it at first — everyone is. Being bad at the start is just the first step to being good later. I'll be right here while you try."
records.what_not_to_say: "Don't be a chicken — just do it!" (Shame never builds courage.)
records.one_action: Shrink the attempt — "Just try for five minutes. If you hate it, we'll stop."
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — "I don't want to try. I'll be bad at it."

records.what_to_say: "You can't do it *yet*. That word matters. What part can you do? Let's start there."
records.what_not_to_say: "Yes you can, it's easy!" (Minimizing the struggle breaks trust.)
records.one_action: Break it down together, then walk through the three questions: What happened? What can we learn? What will we try differently?
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — "I can't do it."

records.situation: Your child loses a game (tears, anger, "this is rigged").
records.what_to_say: "Losing stinks. It's okay to be upset — you cared about it, and caring is good. Want a minute, or want to talk?"
records.what_not_to_say: "It's just a game, stop crying." (Their feelings are real even when the stakes are small.)
records.one_action: When they're calm, ask: "What did the winner do well? Is there one thing you want to practice?" Turn the loss into data.
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — Your child loses a game (tears, anger, "this is rigged").

records.situation: Your child gets in trouble at school.
records.what_to_say: "I heard from school. Before anything else — are you okay? Now tell me what happened, your version."
records.what_not_to_say: "I'm so disappointed in you." (Lead with shame and you'll never hear the real story.)
records.one_action: Separate the behavior from the child — "You're not a bad kid; you made a bad choice. What will you do differently, and how will you make it right?"
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — Your child gets in trouble at school.

records.situation: "I don't want to go to school."
records.what_to_say: "Tell me more — is it something that happened, something coming up, or just a feeling this morning?"
records.what_not_to_say: "Too bad, you're going." (Sometimes they do just have to go — but you'll never know if something's wrong unless you ask first.)
records.one_action: Identify the specific worry and make a plan for it — a script for talking to the teacher, a buddy to find at recess, a note in their backpack.
records.source_reference: Create Childhood Confidence, Appendix B — "I don't want to go to school."
